edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 2, Paris 1844), De corona militis, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Puta denique licere militiam usque ad caussam coronae. Sed et de corona prius dicamus. Laurea ista Apollini vel Libero sacra est: illi, ut deo telorum; huic, ut deo triumphorum. Sic docet Claudius cum et myrto ait milites redimiri solere. Veneris enim myrtum, matris Aeneae, non laurum, etiam amiculae Martis, per Iliam et Romulos Romani. Sed ego Venerem non credo ex hac parte cum Marte Romanam, qua pellicis dolor est. Quum et olea militia coronatur, ad Minervam est idololatria, armorum aeque deam, sed et paci cum Neptuno initae ex hac arbore coronatam. In his erit serti militaris superstitio polluta et polluens, omniaque jam polluentur et caussis. Ecce annua votorum nuncupatio quid videtur? prima in principiis, secunda in capitoliis. Accipe post loca et verba: Tunc Tibi, Jupiter, Bove Cornibus Auro Decoratis Vovimus Esse Futurum. Cujus sententiae vox est? utique negationis. Etiamsi tacet illic Christianus ore, coronatus capite respondit. Eadem laurea in donativi dispensatione denuntiatur plane non gratuita idololatria, aliquibus aureis venditans Christum, ut argenteis Judas. Hoc erit, Non potestis Deo servire et mammonae: mammonae manum tradere, et a Deo absistere? Hoc erit, Reddite quae sunt Caesaris Caesari, et quae Dei Deo: nec hominem Deo reddere, et denarium Caesari auferre? Triumphi laurea foliis struitur, an cadaveribus? lamnis ornatur, an bustis? unguentis delibuitur an lacrymis conjugum et matrum? Fortasse quorumdam et Christianorum: et apud barbaros enim Christus. Qui hanc portaverit in capite caussam, nonne et ipse oppugnavit? Est et alia militia regiarum familiarum. Nam et castrenses appellantur munificiae, et ipsae solemnium Caesareanorum. Sed et tu proinde miles ac servus alterius es: et si duorum, Dei et Caesaris, certe tunc non Caesaris, cum te Deo debes, etiam in communibus, credo, potiori.
pass_a_gloss: Let us assume that military service is allowed up to the point of the crown. But let us first speak about the crown. That laurel is sacred to Apollo or to Liber: to the former, as the god of projectiles; to the latter, as the god of triumphs. Thus Claudius teaches when he says that soldiers are usually redeemed with myrtle. For myrtle is Venus', the mother of Aeneas, not laurel, and also of Mars' loved ones, through Ilium and Romulus, of the Romans. But I do not believe that Venus is on the side of the Romans with Mars, where there is the pain of skin. When also the olive tree is crowned in military service, it is idolatry towards Minerva, the goddess of arms, but also of peace, begun with Neptune, crowned with this tree. In these things, the superstition of the military garland will be polluted and polluting, and all things will now be polluted and causes. Behold, what does the annual vow declaration seem to be? The first in the beginnings, the second in the chapters. Receive the places and words after: Then to You, Jupiter, with a Gold-Decorated Horned Ox, We Vow to Be. What is the voice of this sentence? Certainly of negation. Even if the Christian is silent there with his mouth, the crowned head responds. The same laurel is plainly announced in the dispensation of donatives, not a free idolatry, selling Christ to some for gold, as Judas for silver. This will be, You cannot serve God and mammon: to hand over the hand to mammon, and to stand away from God? This will be, Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's: not to render a man to God, and to take away a denarius from Caesar? Is the triumphal laurel constructed with leaves or with statues? Is it adorned with blades or with busts? Is it anointed with ointments or with the tears of wives and mothers? Perhaps also of some Christians: and Christ is also among the barbarians. He who will have borne this cause on his head, will he not also have fought against it? There is also another military service of royal households. For also the camp gifts are called munificences, and they themselves are of the Caesarean solemnities. But you are also a soldier and a servant of another: and if of two, of God and Caesar, certainly then not of Caesar, when you owe yourself to God, even in common things, I believe, to the more important one.

choices.why: The Latin word 'bustis' refers to statues, not tombs.
The Latin word 'lamnis' refers to blades or metal plates.

bible_refs.note: You cannot serve God and mammon
Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's

pass_b_english: Let us assume that military service is permitted up to the point of the crown. But first, let us speak about the crown. That laurel is sacred to Apollo or to Liber: to Apollo, as the god of projectiles; to Liber, as the god of triumphs. Claudius confirms this when he says that soldiers are customarily wreathed with myrtle. Myrtle belongs to Venus, the mother of Aeneas, not laurel; it also belongs to the loved ones of Mars, through Ilium and Romulus, to the Romans. But I do not believe Venus sides with the Romans alongside Mars in a context where there is the pain of skin. When the olive, too, is used to crown military service, it becomes idolatry directed at Minerva, goddess of arms equally, but also of peace—once peace was established with Neptune, she was crowned from this tree. In these things, the superstition of the military garland is both polluted and polluting, and now all things will be polluted, causes included. Look at the annual declaration of vows—what does it look like? The first part occurs at the *principia*, the second at the *capitolia*. Now take the setting and the words: "Then to you, Jupiter, with a horned ox decorated with gold, we vow to be." Whose voice is that sentence? Unquestionably, the voice of negation. Even if the Christian keeps his mouth silent there, his crowned head answers. That same laurel is openly proclaimed in the distribution of donatives—plainly, not a gratuitous idolatry, but one selling Christ to some for gold, just as Judas did for silver. This will amount to: "You cannot serve God and mammon" (Luke 16:13)—to hand yourself over to mammon and stand apart from God? This will amount to: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's" (Matthew 22:21)—not to render a man to God, and to withhold a denarius from Caesar? Is the triumphal laurel constructed from leaves or from corpses? Is it adorned with blades or with busts? Is it anointed with perfumes or with the tears of wives and mothers? Perhaps even of some Christians: for Christ is also among the barbarians. He who bears this cause on his head—has he not also fought against it? There is also another kind of military service: that of royal households. For the camp largesses are called *munificentiae*, and they themselves belong to the Caesarean solemnities. But you, too, are a soldier and a servant of another; and if you serve two—God and Caesar—then certainly not Caesar, when you owe yourself to God, even in common matters, I believe, to the more important one.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass B correctly identifies and adds the required scripture citations for the quoted passages (Luke 16:13 and Matthew 22:21), which were present in the Latin but not explicitly cited in the source text. Pass A is a faithful gloss. The translation of 'cadaveribus' as 'corpses' in Pass B is correct, whereas Pass A's omission of this word in the 'leaves or...' clause is a minor omission but Pass B restores the full sense.
